NAMING: the book labels V ∝ T at constant P as Gay-Lussac's law (or Charles' law). The standard modern names are Charles' law for V ∝ T at constant P and Gay-Lussac's law for P ∝ T at constant V; the card uses Charles' law and records the book's labelling here.

steps.label: The three laws
lines: temperature) and n (moles) of an ideal gas:
V ∝ T   (P, n constant) — Charles' law
V ∝ n   (P, T constant) — Avogadro's law
steps.why: The ideal gas equation is not a new law — it is three experimental laws about V combined into one, so the derivation must begin by writing all three with their constancy conditions.
common_mistakes: Leaving out Avogadro's law and deriving only PV/T = constant, which loses the n.
Writing the laws without their constant quantities in brackets.
steps.memory_tip: Three laws, one variable each: P from Boyle, T from Charles, n from Avogadro — all acting on V.
steps.margin_note: Each proportionality with its bracket earns credit; the brackets are part of the law.

steps.label: Combining them
lines: Introducing the constant of proportionality R:

lines.text: V = R nT / P   ⟹   PV = nRT

lines: R is the same for all gases — the universal
(molar) gas constant. Hence PV = nRT is the
steps.why: When one quantity is proportional to several others separately, it is proportional to their product. Naming the single constant R and clearing the fraction produces PV = nRT in two lines.
common_mistakes: Writing V ∝ nTP with P multiplied instead of divided.
Introducing a different constant for each law. One combined proportionality takes ONE constant.
steps.memory_tip: One fraction holds all three laws: n and T on top, P below, R in front.
steps.margin_note: The jump from three proportionalities to one is the marked move — write V ∝ nT/P before inserting R.

steps.label: R and its values

lines.text: PV = nRT ,  R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹

lines: R is independent of the amount and the nature
of the gas, so it is called the universal gas
steps.why: The derivation ends by identifying its constant: R takes the same value for every gas, and quoting it in both common unit systems makes the equation ready for numericals.
common_mistakes: Pairing 0.0821 with J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. That number belongs to L atm units.
Omitting the closing statement that R is the same for all gases.
steps.memory_tip: Finish with the values of the constant: 8.314 with joules, 0.0821 with litre-atmospheres.
steps.margin_note: Boxing the equation with one correct R value closes the derivation.

insider_note: Three proportionalities, one combination, one constant — the two middle marks are for the visible jump from V ∝ nT/P to PV = nRT, not for restating the laws.
